summary:
This page has no running text, only two code listings and one figure, all part of section 4.2.4.

**Listing 4.20** plots training and validation accuracy, the figure shown as figure 4.7 on p.145. It starts with `plt.clf()` to clear the current figure (the loss plot from listing 4.19), reads `history.history["accuracy"]` and `history.history["val_accuracy"]`, and reuses the `epochs` range defined in listing 4.19. As before, training is a red dashed line (`"r--"`) and validation a solid blue line (`"b"`), with title, axis labels, a tick at every epoch, and a legend.

**Figure 4.8, Training and validation top-3 accuracy**, is the output of **listing 4.21**, which follows the figure on the page. The listing is identical in structure but reads the keys `"top_3_accuracy"` and `"val_top_3_accuracy"`. Those names exist because the metric object was created on p.143 with `name="top_3_accuracy"`, and Keras prefixes validation versions with `val_`.

In the figure, training top-3 accuracy climbs from about 0.55 at epoch 1 to essentially 1.0 by epoch 12. Validation top-3 accuracy climbs from about 0.68 to around 0.92 by epoch 8 and stays roughly flat (about 0.92-0.93) up to epoch 20. Compared with figure 4.7, where validation accuracy plateaus near 0.82, this means that for roughly 10% of validation newswires the model's first guess is wrong but the right topic is its second or third choice. That is exactly the kind of near-miss that the book said plain accuracy ignores (p.143). As in figures 4.6-4.7, validation performance stops improving long before training performance does; the book's conclusion, that the model overfits after nine epochs, comes on p.147.

concepts.name: Top-k accuracy
concepts.definition: The fraction of samples whose true class is among the model's k most probable classes.
concepts.intuition: Credit for having the right answer on a short list.
concepts.technical: Logged as `top_3_accuracy` / `val_top_3_accuracy` because of the `name` argument of `TopKCategoricalAccuracy(k=3, ...)` (p.143).
concepts.significance: Figure 4.8 shows validation top-3 ≈ 0.92 vs. top-1 ≈ 0.82, revealing many near-miss predictions.
concepts.example: If the true topic is ranked 2nd, top-1 accuracy is 0 and top-3 accuracy is 1 for that sample.
concepts.misconception: A top-3 score of 1.0 on training data does not mean training top-1 accuracy is 1.0; figure 4.7 shows it is about 0.96.

concepts.name: Training History
concepts.definition: Object returned by `fit()` whose `history` dict stores a list of per-epoch values for each monitored metric.
concepts.intuition: A logbook keyed by metric name.
concepts.technical: Key names come from metric names; validation copies get a `val_` prefix. Listings 4.20-4.21 read four of the six keys.
concepts.significance: All of the chapter's curves are drawn from it.
concepts.misconception: Key names are not fixed by Keras for custom metrics; they follow whatever `name` you gave the metric.

parameters.name: "top_3_accuracy" / "val_top_3_accuracy"
parameters.role: History keys created by the custom metric.

pitfalls: A `KeyError` here usually means the metric was created with a different `name` or not included in `compile()`.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written helper, not in the book: one function for all three plots
def plot_metric(history, key, ylabel):
    train = history.history[key]
    val = history.history["val_" + key]
    epochs = range(1, len(train) + 1)
    plt.clf()
    plt.plot(epochs, train, "r--", label="Training " + ylabel)
    plt.plot(epochs, val, "b", label="Validation " + ylabel)
    plt.xlabel("Epochs"); plt.ylabel(ylabel); plt.xticks(epochs)
    plt.legend(); plt.show()

plot_metric(history, "top_3_accuracy", "top-3 accuracy")

deeper.title: Reading figures 4.7 and 4.8 together
deeper.body: Beyond the book: at the plateau, validation top-1 ≈ 0.82 and top-3 ≈ 0.92. So about 10% of validation samples are near misses (true topic ranked 2nd or 3rd) and only about 8% are "far" misses (true topic ranked 4th or lower). On the 1,000 validation samples that is roughly 100 near misses and 80 far misses.

deeper.title: Why training top-3 accuracy saturates at 1.0
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): with about 647k parameters and only 7,982 training samples, the model can fit the training set very closely. By epoch 12 nearly every training sample has its true topic in the top three, so the red curve can no longer reveal anything; only the validation curve remains informative.

misconceptions.claim: Because validation top-3 accuracy does not drop in figure 4.8, there is no overfitting.
misconceptions.correction: Top-3 accuracy is coarse; the validation loss in figure 4.6 (p.145) rises after epoch 9, and the book concludes the model overfits after nine epochs (p.147).

misconceptions.claim: `val_top_3_accuracy` is a built-in key Keras always logs.
misconceptions.correction: It exists only because the metric was added in `compile()` with `name="top_3_accuracy"` and validation data was passed to `fit()`.

questions.question: Why does `history.history` contain the key `"val_top_3_accuracy"`?
options: Keras always logs top-3 accuracy for softmax models
The metric was created with name="top_3_accuracy" and validation_data was passed to fit()
questions.answer: The metric was created with name="top_3_accuracy" and validation_data was passed to fit()
questions.explanation: Keras names history entries after metric names and adds `val_` copies when validation data is given. It is not automatic for softmax models, plotting only reads keys, and the loss choice does not add metrics.

questions.question: What does `plt.clf()` do at the start of listings 4.20 and 4.21?
questions.answer: It clears the current Matplotlib figure so the new curves are not drawn on top of the previous plot.
questions.explanation: Listing 4.19 drew the loss plot; without clearing, the next plot could share the same axes in a script.

questions.question: Using figures 4.7 and 4.8, estimate how many of the 1,000 validation samples are near misses (true topic ranked 2nd or 3rd) at the plateau.
questions.explanation: Top-3 accuracy minus top-1 accuracy is exactly the fraction whose true class is ranked 2nd or 3rd.

questions.question: Training top-3 accuracy approaches 1.0 in figure 4.8. Why is the training curve less useful than the validation curve for deciding when to stop?
questions.answer: Training metrics keep improving as the model fits (and memorizes) the training set, so they say nothing about generalization; only the validation curve shows when performance on unseen data stops improving.
questions.explanation: This is the same reasoning used for IMDb (p.138) and for figures 4.6-4.7.

questions.question: Approximately where does validation top-3 accuracy level off in figure 4.8?
questions.explanation: The blue curve flattens near 0.92-0.93 from about epoch 8. 0.82 is top-1 validation accuracy (figure 4.7), 0.96 is top-1 training accuracy, and 1.00 is training top-3 accuracy.

questions.question: Could you write a single function that plots any metric and its validation counterpart from a `History` object?
questions.answer: Yes: read `history.history[key]` and `history.history["val_" + key]`, build `range(1, len+1)`, and plot both as in listings 4.20-4.21.
questions.explanation: See the illustrative helper in the code notes; it captures the shared pattern of listings 4.19-4.21.
